content: The anecdote is presented as a joke, "Once upon a time," and footnoted to its source, so no reader is misled about what it is. The claim it illustrates does not rest on it: that students reach for fluent scientific words that constrain no expectation. That claim rests on the measured record of physics students who pass exams while holding Aristotelian expectations about motion (Hestenes, Wells & Swackhamer 1992; Hake 1998), which the Fable pass itself cites twice against other essays. A joke that physics teachers pass around because they recognize their students in it is a small piece of evidence in its own right.

The essay draws the distinction the note says it misses. "Under normal circumstances," it says, heat conduction "leads you to anticipate that... that side will feel warmer." The fault is that the student offered it to explain the opposite: "If 'because of heat conduction' can also explain the radiator-adjacent side feeling cooler, then it can explain pretty much anything." The words "used in such fashion" mark the target. Used to predict, heat conduction is a falsifiable hypothesis that the plate falsifies. Used as the students used it, to account for a result it forbids, it is maximum entropy. The essay says both: false as a prediction, empty as the students used it.

quote: Some students guessed convection of air currents, and others guessed strange metals in the plate.
content: The essay does not fault hypothesis generation; its companion essay prescribes it. It walks from "Heat conduction?" to "What does applying the diffusion equation lead me to anticipate? It sure doesn't lead me to anticipate that the side of a metal plate farther away from a radiator would feel warmer. I notice that I am confused." The students' failure was that none of them noticed the result was anomalous, "none stooping so low as to say 'I don't know' or 'This seems impossible.'" Expert diagnosticians are marked out by noticing when the data fail to fit their hypothesis. And the physicist's measurements were available to any student with a hand and a clock. The essay's point is that none of them thought to ask for them.
